overview: I3104 ties night instrument cockpit setup to terminal instrument procedures. The event standard is to brief and fly SID, RVFAC, ILS/LOC, and point-to-point tasks while keeping night setup, minimums discipline, and emergency-procedure branch logic ahead of the aircraft.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Night cockpit setup is about preserving the scan, protecting night adaptation, and making every needed chart, light, and control usable before workload rises.

children.text: Set interior lighting early enough to read instruments and charts without washing out dark adaptation or making the display picture harder to interpret.
Know where utility, map, and kneeboard lighting are before the approach sequence; do not discover the lighting plan during a frequency change or missed approach.
Dim bright displays gradually and keep the standby instruments and backup lighting in the scan.
At night, a cockpit lighting, display, radio, or electrical problem can become a recovery-timing problem faster than it would in daylight.
Use exterior lighting with airfield courtesy and local procedures, especially around ground crews, other aircraft, and low-visibility taxi conditions.
If field orientation becomes uncertain, stop or stabilize the aircraft and re-sort the picture instead of continuing while unsure.

items.text: A SID is a published IFR departure procedure that provides obstacle clearance and transitions the aircraft from the terminal area toward the en route structure.

children.text: Before takeoff, review the entire SID, terrain, hazards, climb gradient, crossing restrictions, transition, and lost-communication or emergency-return implications.
Set NAVAIDs, displays, and courses required for the first turns and altitude restrictions. If FMS use is authorized, confirm the loaded procedure matches the clearance.
Keep the primary recovery approach available in case the departure must become an emergency return.
Fly the cleared procedure, not just the chart title. Understand whether the clearance includes climb-via language, radar vectors, or a named transition.
If the SID requires a climb gradient above standard, confirm aircraft performance before accepting the plan.
Common errors are briefing only the first heading, missing an altitude or crossing restriction, and launching with the wrong NAVAID or display source selected.

items.text: RVFAC uses radar vectors to place the aircraft on the final approach course, which can reduce terminal workload only if orientation and setup stay ahead.

children.text: Approach control vectors using minimum vectoring altitude charts, but the pilot still keeps terrain and procedure SA.
Crosscheck assigned altitudes against the approach, NAVAIDs, and chart picture; query ATC if the vector or altitude does not make sense.
Maintain the last assigned heading and altitude until established on the approach or cleared otherwise.
Use 200 KIAS on downwind, 150 KIAS on base, and 200 KIAS on extended final or dogleg until within about 15 NM unless directed otherwise.
Tune and identify the appropriate NAVAID, verify PFD source/configuration, and set the final approach course in the CDI.
If a FAF is depicted, transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF when heading is within 90 degrees of the final approach course.
If no FAF is depicted, transition once established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach.

items.text: ILS/LOC approaches use localizer guidance for precise lateral control; ILS adds glideslope for a precision approach, while LOC-only is nonprecision.

children.text: The localizer is much more sensitive than VOR guidance, about 1.25 degrees per dot, so course corrections must be small and prompt.
Set the published front course to avoid reverse-sensing errors and confirm the PFD source changes to LOC.
If the localizer is inoperative, the ILS is not authorized. If the glideslope is unavailable, fly the LOC procedure using nonprecision rules and minimums.
For a single-piloted T-6B, do not plan below the applicable absolute single-pilot minimums even if the charted ILS minimums are lower.
Use D LIDS: DME hold if required, localizer tune/identify/monitor, inbound course set, display source to LOC, and speed appropriate to the transition.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF with an intercept angle at or below 90 degrees, or when the glideslope comes alive if that occurs first.
At glideslope intercept, use about 24 percent torque, descend on course and glideslope to DA/DH, and remember that pitch primarily controls airspeed while power controls glideslope.
At DA/DH, decide: land if the runway environment is in sight and landing is safe; otherwise execute the missed approach. Do not level at DA/DH.
For LOC-only, start backup timing at the nonprecision FAF if timing is available, then descend with about 20 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and no more than 1000 FPM.
Lead the MDA level-off by about 100 feet, use about 42 percent torque to stabilize, and maintain MDA until the MAP.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, re-intercept and do not descend below the FAF altitude until on scale.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs inside the FAF, turn to reestablish, climb to the appropriate MAP altitude while respecting restrictions, and execute the missed approach at the MAP.
If more than 1 dot below glideslope before the MAP, do not descend below LOC MDA until reestablished; if more than 2 dots above glideslope, continue as LOC-only.

items.text: PTP is a VOR/DME or VORTAC technique for navigating directly from present position to a radial/DME fix without radar vectors.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID, then set the desired radial in the CDI even if that is not the heading you will fly.
Visualize the station at the center of the compass card. Put the larger DME on the outer edge at its radial and the smaller DME proportionally closer to the center.
Split the bearing-pointer and course-pointer heads for the initial heading, favoring the bearing pointer when going to smaller DME and the course pointer when going to larger DME.
Use the pencil method or compass-card picture to update heading as the line to the fix changes.
If DME will arrive first, use the 90-degree benchmark to slow DME change; do not turn the maneuver into an arc.
If the radial arrives first, track inbound or outbound on the radial to the fix.
A bearing-pointer head above the 90-degree benchmark means DME is decreasing; below the benchmark means DME is increasing.
Common errors are delaying the initial turn, plotting the reciprocal radial, failing to update heading, or tracking the radial too early.

items.text: Any emergency procedure in this event should be briefed as a decision process: maintain control, execute memory items when required, back up with the checklist, coordinate with ATC, and choose the correct recovery branch.

children.text: For fuel-system emphasis, low fuel pressure and high fuel flow both point toward a PEL rather than extended troubleshooting.
For low fuel pressure, execute the PEL and place the boost pump ON. If the FUEL PX warning remains illuminated, the high-pressure fuel pump is suction feeding and engine operation is time-limited.
Unless a greater emergency exists, do not reset an open BOOST PUMP circuit breaker.
For high fuel flow, execute a PEL. Reducing power when ITT remains within limits may risk flameout, while high power with high ITT may aggravate the malfunction.
At night or in IMC, declare early when needed and tell ATC what recovery you need before radio, lighting, or display workload steals the scan.
A strong EP brief explains the cue, the immediate action, the N/W/C that changes the answer, and the follow-on branch: continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

studyNotes.summary: Set the night cockpit before workload rises, then fly SID, RVFAC, ILS/LOC, and PTP tasks while keeping emergency-procedure branch logic close at hand.

summary: Night cockpit setup, SID, RVFAC, ILS/LOC approaches, point-to-point navigation, and emergency-procedure decision making.
